To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the Hoare rules for program verification can be augmented to support explanation generation, and that the generated explanations are based on an analysis of labels that are maintained through the processing steps of the calculus.
(1) the labels can be used as an explanation mechanism for the VCs and that (2) this approach can be implemented as a tool that is integrated with a verification system.

(1) the Hoare calculus can be extended with labels that can be used to explain the verification conditions; (2) the labels can be generated automatically by a tool; and (3) the explanations can be customized and generated automatically.
In summary, our research is concerned with
(1) the construction of VCs and their proofs, (2) the labeling and explanation of VCs, and (3) their integration into a verification environment.
the following question: How to make the VCs more comprehensible and usable?

the following questions: How to systematically extend the Hoare rules so that they support the generation of explanations? What is the structure and purpose of the explanations? What is their relation to the VCs and their proofs? How do the explanations support understanding and debugging?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
our approach is able to explain verification conditions.
the verification conditions are sound, i.e., they are valid if and only if the original program satisfies its specification.
we have shown that it is feasible to generate a complete explanation of the verification conditions for a Hoare-style program proof.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we can explain VCs in a way that is independent of the underlying logic, the underlying proof method, the underlying program, and the underlying programming language.
the Hoare rules are extended with labels and the labels are used to generate explanations of the VCs.
the labels can be used to generate explanations that are both accurate and concise.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a formal calculus can be extended to support the construction and explanation of verification conditions in a systematic and modular way.
a systematic extension of a verification calculus with labels can be used to generate explanations of verification conditions.
the Hoare rules can be extended with labels in a way that supports a systematic generation of explanations of VCs and proofs.
